---
title: "Getting set up"
subtitle: "Everything you need to run the soil texture analysis, from gamma rays to clay and silt."
author: "Xyza Vasily Dela Pena"
---

This guide gets your computer ready to run the Raasdorf soil texture notebook. You will install Python, an editor, and five packages. It takes about 15 minutes.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will have at the end
- Python installed
- An editor (Positron or VS Code) that can run notebooks
- A clean, project-only Python environment
- A notebook that runs without errors
:::

## Install Python

Download Python 3.10 or later from [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/) and run the installer.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Windows users
On the first screen of the installer, tick **Add python.exe to PATH**. If you forget, your terminal won't find Python and the next steps will fail.
:::

To check it worked, open a terminal and run:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
python --version
```

You should see something like `Python 3.12.x`. On macOS and Linux, the command may be `python3` instead of `python`. If so, use `python3` everywhere in this guide.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Linux (Debian / Ubuntu)
You also need the tool that creates virtual environments:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
sudo apt install python3-venv
```
:::

## Install an editor

You need somewhere to open the notebook and run the code. Pick one. Both are free and both work well.

### Option 1: Positron (recommended)

Download [Positron](https://positron.posit.co) and install it. It is built for data science: you see your code, your plots, and your variables all in one window, and it runs Python and R side by side.

Once it is installed, open it and check that it found Python: look at the interpreter picker in the bottom status bar. If you don't see your Python version there, click the picker and choose it from the list.

### Option 2: Visual Studio Code

If you already use [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com), you can stay with it. Positron is built on the same foundation, so it will feel familiar. Install these two extensions from the Extensions panel:

- **Python** (by Microsoft)
- **Jupyter** (by Microsoft)

Without the Jupyter extension, VS Code can't open `.ipynb` notebooks.

## Get the project files

Go to the [project repository](https://github.com/your-username/your-repo) on GitHub, click **Code** -> **Download ZIP**, and unzip it.

If you already use git, you can clone it instead:


```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
```
The folder contains the notebook (`soil_texture_raasdorf.ipynb`) and a file called `requirements.txt`. That file is the list of packages we use.

## Open the project folder

Open the whole project folder in your editor, not just the notebook file.

- **Positron or VS Code**: `File` -> `Open Folder…`, then choose the project folder.

This matters because the next step creates the environment *inside* this folder, and the editor needs to be looking at the same place.

## Create your environment

Think of a virtual environment as a clean lab bench just for this project. The packages you install on it stay on it, so they never clash with other Python projects on your computer.

Open a terminal inside your editor (`Terminal` -> `New Terminal`). It opens in the project folder already.

**Step 1.** Create the environment. This makes a hidden folder called `.venv`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
python -m venv .venv
```

**Step 2.** Switch it on:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Windows

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
.venv\Scripts\activate
```

## macOS / Linux

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
source .venv/bin/activate
```

:::

You should now see `(.venv)` at the start of your terminal line. That means the bench is ready.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Windows PowerShell says "running scripts is disabled"?
Run this once, then try the activate command again:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
```
:::

## Install the packages

With `(.venv)` showing, run:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

This reads `requirements.txt` and installs everything the notebook needs. It can take a few minutes the first time.

Here is what is in that file and why:

| Package | What we use it for |
|---|---|
| `numpy` | Numbers and arrays, plus the permutation tests |
| `pandas` | Reading the CSV files and working with tables |
| `matplotlib` | Every figure in the analysis |
| `scipy` | Linear regressions and nearest-neighbour matching of GPS points |
| `statsmodels` | Multiple regression, VIF, and ANCOVA |
| `ipykernel` | Lets your editor run the notebook with this environment |

If you would rather install them by hand, this does the same thing:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
pip install numpy pandas matplotlib scipy statsmodels ipykernel
```

## Tell the notebook which Python to use

Open `soil_texture_raasdorf.ipynb`. In the top-right corner, click the kernel (or interpreter) picker and choose the one that points to `.venv`.

If you don't see it, close the notebook, restart the editor, and try again. The `.venv` environment appears once the editor has noticed the folder.

## Point the notebook to your data

The notebook reads three CSV files from a folder. In the early setup cell you will find a line like this:

```{.python filename="Notebook"}
BASE_DIR = r"E:\Gamma Ray Sensor\Raasdorf_July 22, 2026\Soil_Texture"
```

Change it to the folder where **your** copies of the files live:

- `Soil_data_HOAL.csv`
- `Trial.csv`
- `concentrations_NNLS_output.csv`

## Check everything works

Run this in a notebook cell:

::: {#065503c9 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib
import scipy
import statsmodels

for pkg in [np, pd, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels]:
    print(f"{pkg.__name__:12} {pkg.__version__}")
```
:::


If you see five package names with version numbers and no errors, you are set up and ready to go.

## If something goes wrong

| What you see | What to try |
|---|---|
| `python` is not recognized | Reinstall Python and tick **Add python.exe to PATH** (Windows), or use `python3` (macOS / Linux). |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'` | The notebook is using the wrong Python. Pick the `.venv` kernel (see above), and check `(.venv)` shows in your terminal. |
| `pip` is not recognized | Use `python -m pip install -r requirements.txt` instead. |
| `FileNotFoundError` when loading data | Check that `BASE_DIR` points to the right folder and the file names match exactly. |

## Cheatsheet

Run these in the terminal, with the project open.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `python -m venv .venv` | Creates the environment (once). |
| `.venv\Scripts\activate` | Switches it on (Windows). |
| `source .venv/bin/activate` | Switches it on (macOS / Linux). |
| `pip install -r requirements.txt` | Installs everything the project needs. |
| `pip list` | Shows what is installed. |
| `pip freeze > requirements.txt` | Saves your exact package versions to the file. |
| `deactivate` | Switches the environment off. |

You only need the first three commands and `pip install -r` once. After that, you just activate the environment each time you come back.
